claim: Jordan et al. explicitly identify min-max normalization over algorithms' own mean scores -- g(i,j) = (mu_ij - min_i' mu_i'j) / (max_i' mu_i'j - min_i' mu_i'j) -- as a normalization technique that does not correct for nonlinear scaling and is not robust to a single outlier algorithm setting the min or max.
stance_target: min-max normalization is fragile to outlier entries setting the range used as the normalizer
scope_conditions: RL benchmark cross-environment aggregation using min-max normalized algorithm mean performance (Bellemare et al. 2013; Balduzzi et al. 2018 style normalization)
quoted_support: This normalization technique does not correct for nonlinear scaling of performance. As a result algorithms could be near 0 or 1 if there is an outlier algorithm that does very well or poorly. For example, one could introduce a terrible algorithm that just chooses one action the whole time. This makes the environment seem easier as all scores would be near 1 except for this bad algorithm. We would like the evaluation procedure to be robust to the addition of poor algorithms.

claim: Fixed [0,1] range normalization based on absolute min/max scores per environment causes normalized performances to cluster in different (non-comparable) regions of [0,1] across environments, since the min/max endpoints (e.g., -100 to 10 vs. 10 to 1000) are arbitrary per-environment quantities unrelated to actual task difficulty.
stance_target: min-max/range normalization does not produce a genuinely common, comparable scale across tasks
scope_conditions: RL cross-environment score normalization, general critique independent of the specific benchmark
quoted_support: On the first environment, algorithms will tend to have a normalized performance near 1 and in the second case most algorithms will have a normalized performance near 0. So in the second environment algorithms will likely appear worse than algorithms in the first regardless of how close to optimal they are. This means the normalized performances are not really comparable.

claim: The performance-ratio normalization technique is sensitive to the location and scale of the raw performance metric on each environment -- e.g., an environment with scores in [0,1] produces larger apparent differences than one with scores in [1000,1001] -- and combined with an arithmetic mean it can produce arbitrary rankings depending on which algorithm is used as the denominator.
stance_target: raw-score-scale-sensitive normalization techniques distort cross-task aggregate comparisons
scope_conditions: Performance-ratio normalization as used with the Arcade Learning Environment (Mnih et al. 2015; Machado et al. 2018)
quoted_support: This ratio is sensitive to the location and scale of the performance metric on each environment, such that an environment with scores in the range [0,1] will produce larger differences than those on the range [1000,1001]. ... A critical flaw in the performance ratio is that it can produce an arbitrary ordering of algorithms when combined with the arithmetic mean, meaning a different algorithm in the denominator could change the relative rankings.

claim: A nonexploitative evaluation procedure requires that no algorithm be favored merely by performing well on an over-represented subset of environments or 'by abusing a particular score normalization method' -- explicitly naming normalization-method exploitability as a criterion evaluation procedures must satisfy.
stance_target: normalization/aggregation choice is itself a source of exploitable bias that a rigorous evaluation methodology must guard against
scope_conditions: General requirements for RL algorithm evaluation methodology
quoted_support: the evaluation procedure should be nonexploitative (Balduzzi et al., 2018), meaning no algorithm should be favored by performing well on an over-represented subset of environments or by abusing a particular score normalization method.

claim: The paper proposes 'performance percentiles' -- normalizing an algorithm's score on each environment by the CDF of a mixture/reference distribution rather than by the min/max range -- as a more robust alternative because CDF-based normalization is a monotonic probability-integral transform that equally distributes difficulty across [0,1] without being anchored to two extreme (and potentially outlier-driven) data points.
stance_target: min-max normalization is an adequate way to place per-task scores on a common comparable scale
scope_conditions: Proposed alternative normalization technique for RL cross-environment aggregation
quoted_support: The probability integral transform shows that projecting a random variable through its CDF transforms the variable to be uniform on [0,1]. Thus, normalizing an algorithm's performance by its CDF will equally distribute and represent a linear scaling of difficulty across [0,1].

claim: The tune-and-report data collection method and standard aggregation practices in RL do not properly quantify uncertainty, contributing to inconsistent, hard-to-replicate reported performance results across the field.
stance_target: the inconsistency of RL benchmark results stems from flawed evaluation/aggregation metrics, not just noisy experiments
scope_conditions: General RL evaluation methodology critique, ICML 2020
quoted_support: we argue that the inconsistency of performance stems from the use of flawed evaluation metrics.
